cells.tense: You are passing something on right now and the form of it is still yours to move.
cells.act: find the centre and hold it while things move
cells.ask: This week take something you hand on often. Find what has to stay in it, hold that steady, and change one other word around it.
cells.core:
You hand a meaning forward and the way you hand it keeps shifting — a word swapped, a step loosened so someone unlike you can still walk in. The whole pattern is visible while you stand inside it, so what travels doesn't have to be frozen to stay true. Held this way, people belong without having to agree, and the meaning outlives its own wording.

Find what has to stay in the thing you pass on — the part that holds steady while everything around it moves — change one other word, and leave the change alone after that. That centre wasn't yours to guard. You get to teach, and the teaching gets to stay alive in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You can hand a meaning on and still let it move.

cells.tense: By next season you will be defending the old form as if the form were the meaning itself.
cells.act: let one structure collapse that could not hold
cells.ask: Name a rule around what you pass on that you keep from habit rather than conviction, and stop propping it — no announcement, just no longer held up.
cells.core:
Where you hand a meaning forward, you've started bracing — insisting the old form is the meaning rather than its wrapping, and asking for agreement you once didn't need. Every window gets sealed at the edges, and what was meant to travel stands still. The pattern is still visible to you; you're refusing to let it breathe. Tightness this strong usually guards something loved, and it costs what the meaning was for.

Find a rule around how you pass this on that you keep up out of habit rather than because it's true. Stop propping it, quietly, with nothing said about why. What couldn't hold will come down; what was the real thing will still stand. The teaching gets lighter, and you get to hear the room again.
cells.sheetLine: You are holding up the form and calling it the meaning.

cells.tense: You have been working things out alone, and the framework you carry has nothing around it to hand to.
cells.act: trace the pattern across the last few times
cells.ask: Put the last three things you worked out into one shape — the move they share, no details — and stop once it's written.
cells.core:
You see how things work underneath, and you do it from outside any shared framework, so each generation around you reinvents what you worked out years back. What you understand, you understand alone. The pattern stays in your hands and doesn't leave them, and the little that gets handed on walks out uncredited. Seeing the whole shape is here in you. Lately it stands at the door.

Put the last three things you figured out or said into one line — the move you keep making, none of the details. Not to fix anything; write it and stop. That line is the part of teaching that comes before words get chosen, and writing it down puts the shape where you can see that it's yours.
cells.sheetLine: You see the shape of everything and keep it to yourself.

cells.tense: You are handing something on while the story you tell has you standing on the side.
cells.act: blend the two things instead of choosing one
cells.ask: Next time a person brings you a muddle, set the old way and your own way side by side, and don't pick for them.
cells.core:
Something goes out through you and you have your back to it. You explain how a thing works, or you show someone the move they were missing, and you file it as filling time — nothing, obviously nothing. You see the whole pattern, so what you say next tends to be what someone needed, and you don't count it as having handed anything to anyone. The one who does it doesn't know.

Let both the old way and your own way sit in front of someone, side by side, and don't choose for them. Blending is what you do already and have filed as nothing. The meaning moves through you either way; naming it is only the light going on where the work has been happening.
cells.sheetLine: You are already the one handing it on.

attempts.check: The draft asserts several things the record does not support: that the person has already taught specific people, that a particular structure is definitely false, that 'windows sealed' names an event rather than a tendency. A reader could reasonably say: 'I don't teach anyone' or 'the structure isn't false, it's just mine.' The asks survive being wrong because each is small, private, and teaches the person something regardless; none requires a safe person, money, or a verdict about anyone else. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'cartography is what you offer' — it is a line that sounds like the house rather than the person, so I have cut or kept it only where it sits in the second person's own terms.
